title: Peaky traffic, link fragmentation, and NCCL microburst journal
content:
Objective:
This notebook documents experiments and observations about how bursty ("peaky") inference traffic interacts with interconnect packetization and NCCL collective behavior, producing transient tail-latency spikes on multi-GPU deployments. The goal is to identify practical mitigations (OS/NIC tunables, NCCL settings, request shaping) and a reproducible test harness for future regressions.

Context & motivation:
We observed intermittent P99 regressions on multi-host 8x-GPU pools serving a 30B encoder-decoder model under real customer traffic patterns. The anomalies are not explained by steady-state throughput — they correlate with short, high-amplitude bursts of concurrent requests (10s-100s of requests within 50–300ms). Hypothesis: packetization + NIC/IB hardware buffering causes link-level fragmentation that interacts badly with NCCL chunking/reduction algorithms, triggering microbursts and collective synchronization stalls.

Testbed summary:
- Nodes: 2x identical hosts, each with 8x A100 80GB (NVLink mesh intra-node), Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 12.1, NCCL 2.18.03.
- Interconnect: Mellanox HDR200 (200Gbps IB) between nodes, default mtu=4096, driver MLNX_OFED 5.6.
- OS tuning baseline: default TCP, TSO/LSO enabled, RPS disabled.
- Serving runtime: Redwood dev build (commit a1b2c3d), pipeline-parallel model split into 4 stages (2 ranks/node), tensor-parallel=2, KV cache warm.
- Workloads: two synthetic arrival patterns — (A) steady Poisson at 150 req/s, (B) peaky: 10 bursts/min, each burst = 200 concurrent single-token continuation requests arriving within 80ms window.
- Measurements: token throughput, p50/p95/p99 latency, NIC counters (bytes/packets, skb drops, XMIT wakeups), ibv_rc counters, NCCL debug traces (S_COLL and chunk timing), CPU runqueue metrics, dmesg for buffer overflows.

Key observations (high level):
1) Baseline steady workload: P99 ~= 78ms, low variance.
2) Peaky workload baseline: frequent P99 spikes to 300–520ms coincident with packet bursts. Spikes correlate with host-level transmit queue elongation and nccl op stalls (collective wait times inflate).
3) Packet-level analysis: bursts produce large numbers of small packets due to application-level writes + TCP segmentation and NIC coalescing misalignment. The RDMA verbs layer reports many small WRs (work requests) resulting in smaller RDMA messages than expected, increasing number of NCCL chunks and increasing synchronization points.
4) Link fragmentation: when multiple ranks simultaneously produce many small WRs, switch-level buffering and PCIe host staging saturate transiently — we observed microburst-driven queue depth jumps on NICs and IB ports.

Counterfactual experiments and results:
- Increase TX coalescing (disable TSO/LSO): reduces number of tiny packets leaving the NIC but increases CPU overhead. Result: P99 reduced from 300–520ms to 140–210ms during bursts, at 10–15% higher CPU usage on host.
- Larger MTU/jumbo frames (mtu=9000): modest improvement in packetization but only when paired with TCP seg offload disabled — isolated MTU change gave small gains. Combined with TSO off, P99 ~120ms.
- NCCL environmental knobs: set NCCL_BUFFSIZE and NCCL_RING_CHUNK to larger sizes (2x default) to reduce number of chunks per collective. Result: collective scheduling overhead falls, P99 ~130ms. But too-large chunk sizes hurt steady throughput for longer sequences.
- NCCL_P2P_DISABLE=1 (force ring fallback): eliminated some cross-node synchronization stalls, reducing variance, but throughput dropped ~8% steady-state for our topology. Tradeoff depending on SLOs.
- Host-level pacing: adding a thin request-shaper in the runtime that spreads arrivals across 20ms windows (soft smoothing) dramatically reduced spikes: P99 during bursts ~96ms. This is the most effective mitigation with minimal infra change.
- RDMA QP tuning: increasing max_send_wr and max_recv_wr on QPs reduced ibv completion queue pressure; P99 improved ~10–15ms over baseline non-tuned.

Microtrace example (single burst):
- t=0ms: burst of 200 requests from LB -> worker ranks begin decoding; many small writes issued to NIC.
- t=15–35ms: NIC TX queue length jumps, ibv_post_send rates spike; packets appear as 64–256B.
- t=36–50ms: NCCL collective enters wait on chunk 7 because peer hasn't posted corresponding WR; local compute finishes but GPU stalls waiting for network chunk.
- t=50–90ms: host CPU handles increased softirq load, TSO attempts to aggregate, but ramp causes further delay; completion events delivered in clumps, causing SC-collection to resume, but with overshoot latency.
- t=90–120ms: recovery and burst drains; tail observed in p99.

Interpretation and root causes (working hypothesis):
- The dominant failure mode is not raw bandwidth exhaustion but synchrony amplification: many small RDMA/TCP writes cause NCCL to split collectives into many small chunks. The mismatch between when each rank posts its WR and when other ranks receive completions creates extra synchronization stalls. Switch/NIC buffering and OS coalescing add jitter that amplifies this into long microburst-induced stalls.

Mitigations and recommendations (ranked):
1) Runtime-level request smoothing: implement an adaptive micro-throttle that detects rising request concurrency and spreads scheduling across 10–50ms (configurable). Low implementation cost, largest win for tail.
2) Default NCCL profile tuned for bursty inference: increase default chunk size and raise NCCL buffer allocations with heuristics for short-sequence inference loads. Add as a profile option in serving runtime.
3) Expose NIC pacing controls and recommended OS knobs in deployment docs: show tradeoffs for disabling TSO/LSO vs CPU cost.
4) Add RDMA/QP tuning to node bootstrap (max_send_wr / completion queue sizing) and include monitoring alerts when CQ overflows approach threshold.
5) Scheduler placement hinting: where feasible, collocate ranks that exchange high-frequency small WRs on the same host (prefer NVLink) to avoid IB hops for the most chatty collectives. Incorporate placement advice into Dedicated deployment planner.

Follow-ups and experiments to run next:
- Quantify CPU overhead vs tail reduction curve for different combinations of TSO/LSO, TCP_NODELAY, and HW offloads. Produce a 2D Pareto front.
- Try RDMA message coalescing at the verbs layer (post larger aggregated WRs) in a controlled patch to the low-level transport and measure the NCCL chunk count and p99.
- Evaluate effect on longer generation sequences (>=1024 tokens) — ensure chunk growth doesn't regress throughput.
- Implement lightweight runtime pacing prototype and A/B test across a customer fleet to measure SLO impact.

Quick action items (owners):
- Daniel Kim: prototype adaptive micro-throttle in serving runtime (RFC by 2025-11-14).
- Aisha Patel: add NCCL profile option and perf tests for chunk sizing (PR draft by 2025-11-17).
- Michael Chen: RDMA/QP tuning recommendations for bootstrap scripts + monitoring (ticket RW-1241).

Appendix: useful commands & captures used during investigation:
- tcpdump (small sample): showed many 64–256B payloads during burst windows.
- ethtool -S <iface> to capture tx queue lengths.
- ibv_rc_pingpong variations to approximate WR size sensitivity.
- NCCL_DEBUG=INFO logs (timestamped) to correlate chunk timing.

Notes: this document is intentionally a working journal — many ideas are exploratory. The runtime smoothing approach appears to deliver the best pragmatic win with limited infra change; NCCL and RDMA tuning are valuable for additional robustness. We'll converge on a recommended set of deploy defaults once follow-up experiments quantify steady-state tradeoffs.

End of journal.
